title: Flatten Up to a Depth
statement:
You get a nested array arr whose items are integers or further arrays of the same kind, and a number n. Write your own version of Array.prototype.flat(n) without calling it.

The items of arr itself sit at depth 0, the items inside one of its sub-arrays sit at depth 1, and so on. A sub-array found at depth d is replaced by its own items only if d < n; otherwise it is kept as it is. Return the new array; keep the items in their original order.

examples.why: Only the depth-0 array [2, [3, [4]]] is opened. Its item [3, [4]] sits at depth 1, which is not below n = 1.
Arrays at depths 0 and 1 are opened; [4] sits at depth 2 and stays.
Opening [] adds nothing. Opening [[]] leaves its inner [] at depth 1, which is kept.

constraints: 0 ≤ total number of integers and arrays ≤ 100 000
hints: Walk the items of arr in order. An integer is copied as is. What decides whether an array is copied or opened?
Its depth. Recurse into an array at depth d with a smaller remaining budget n − 1, and copy it whole when the budget is 0.
To avoid deep recursion, use an explicit stack of (array, index, depth) frames, which is what the call stack would hold anyway.

explain.intuition:
Each array you open spends one level of the budget n. So a recursive helper walk(items, budget) does it: for each item, if it is an array and budget > 0, call walk(item, budget − 1) to spread its items into the output; otherwise push the item as it is. Order is preserved because you finish one sub-array before moving to the next sibling.

The iterative version replaces the call stack with an explicit stack of frames [array, nextIndex, depth]. This is the same depth-first walk a DOM tree walker does, and it is how you avoid a stack overflow when the nesting is deep.
steps: Create an empty out array and push the frame [arr, 0, 0] on a stack.
Look at the top frame. If its index has passed the end, pop it and continue.
Otherwise take the next item and advance the index.
If the item is an array and the frame's depth is < n, push [item, 0, depth + 1]. Otherwise push the item into out.
When the stack is empty, return out.
pitfalls: Opening arrays at depth n too (using ≤). With n = 1, [3, [4]] in the first example must stay whole.
Dropping empty arrays that should be kept: an empty array at depth ≥ n is still an item.
Pushing all items of a frame onto the stack at once without reversing them, which flips the order.

solutions.title: Recursive spread
solutions.idea: Open an array when the remaining depth budget is above 0, recursing with one less.

solutions.title: Explicit stack of frames
solutions.idea: Simulate the recursion with [array, index, depth] frames so deep nesting cannot overflow the call stack.

followups: Make it a generator that yields items lazily, so a caller can stop early.
